references.text: Originally, God gave humans only plants for food. In Gen 9:3 this is expanded to also include animals – a significant change in dietary laws after the flood.
The psalm praises God for his provision of food for humans – crops, bread, and wine – and testifies to God's generous care for creation.
The Mosaic law introduces the distinction between clean and unclean animals, narrowing the broad permission to eat all living creatures that was given after the flood.
Peter's vision that all animals are clean abolishes the dietary laws of the Mosaic law and confirms the original broad permission to eat all kinds of animals.
The apostles' instruction to Gentile Christians to abstain from blood and meat of strangled animals shows that certain restrictions on food intake still apply under the new covenant.
Paul warns against those who forbid certain foods, affirming that everything God has created is good and should not be rejected – in line with the broad permission given after the flood.
Permission to slaughter and eat meat freely, reflecting the broad allowance to eat animals.
Contrast between the original vegetarian order (1:30) and the new permission to eat meat after the flood (9:3).
The direct theological contrast: a gift of only plants (1:29) versus a gift of all living things (9:3).
Narrative and theological connection: the purposeful provision of animals (8:17) and their new role as food for humans (9:3).
